source.title_on_document: Examining Human-AI Collaboration for Co-Writing Constructive Comments Online

supplement.where: Appendix A, pp. 30-33, Tables 11-20 and Figure 7. No external supplement identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A includes thread titles, generation settings and prompts, Figure 7, and Tables 11-20 (pp. 30-33). Tables 15 and 17 give pairwise and signed-rank tests; Tables 16 and 18 give length-adjusted ANCOVAs; Table 19 gives country-specific linguistic values. Main-text Table 8 (p. 18) gives cross-writer similarity and vocabulary-diversity results. No SD, SE, or confidence interval for the core diversity contrasts is supplied.

paper_design_summary: A preparatory validation study, a small instrument-development pilot, and a perception experiment preceded a Prolific experiment that randomly assigned Indian and US writers to independent writing or GPT-4 revision assistance. The writing experiment reports 103 analyzed writers; their final comments were scored for constructiveness, linguistic properties, and similarity across writers (pp. 2, 10-12, 14-19). A separate evaluation panel scored these outputs and researcher-generated AI comments; its AI-only versus human-only benchmark is retained as linked context evidence.

studies.label: Phase 1 preparatory validation of GPT-4 argumentation styles

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each individual annotator received a randomly selected thread and randomly selected GPT-4 comments; neutral annotators also received randomly selected comment stances. Logical and dialectical comment types are stimulus conditions, not AI assistance assigned to writers (pp. 7-8). Exposure to both argumentation styles within each annotator and condition order are not specified; structure is therefore null.
assignment.quote: Then, we showed them either one randomly selected homophobic or Islamophobic thread, along with four randomly selected LLM-generated comments written for that thread.
assignment.prereg_locator: Not stated in full text or Appendix A (pp. 1-33).

arms.name: Human-written comments (control)
arms.description: People wrote without external assistance, including the Internet or ChatGPT. 104 comments are reported; the analyzed number of people in this arm is not explicitly stated (pp. 10, 12).

participants.exclusions: The analyzed writing sample is 103 people: the Introduction reports 103 writers (p. 2), and Table 5 lists US 52 and India 51 who completed the writing task (p. 12). Recruitment counts are not explicitly assignment counts, so n_randomized is null. Arm-specific people counts are not inferred from comments. The reference to 87 participants incorporating suggestions on p. 16 has an unresolved denominator/unit and is not used as an independent people count.

ai_tool.how_used: Draft at least 20 words, then select provided prompts or write a custom prompt; at least one model request required. The rewriting prompt included thread, country, stance, and draft. Participants could accept, reject, regenerate, or edit (pp. 10-11 and Figure 2). Appendix generation settings refer to Phase 1 stimuli; applicability to the live revision interface is not stated.

task.description: Write one constructive English comment on a homophobic thread and one on an Islamophobic thread relevant to the writer's country, expressing their own stance. Final comments had to be at least 50 words. This task is in scope through similarity across writers, not an explicit originality rating (pp. 6, 10-12, 17-19).
task.duration: No fixed limit stated. Mean writing time: test 5.17 minutes; control 6.71 minutes (p. 16, Section 4.2.1).

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity across writers
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Semantic similarity between different writers on the same thread and with the same stance (pp. 17-18, Section 4.2.3). Methods identify all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for semantic similarity on p. 12 in the draft-final analysis; the cross-writer section does not independently restate the model. No explicit primary-outcome designation, exact nonsignificant p-value, SD, SE, or CI is supplied. The statistical observation unit is not specified: the source does not establish whether the Mann-Whitney tests use individual text-pair scores or aggregated similarities, so unit and n_units are null.

contrasts.reported: Control 0.41; test 0.42. Table 8 prints a dash under statistics, and the text reports no significant difference. No SD, SE, exact p-value, or test statistic is printed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 17-18, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8.

diversity_detail.metric: Semantic similarity; higher raw scores mean lower diversity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer is named in Methods (p. 12); Section 4.2.3 does not independently restate the cross-writer model.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Different writers within the same arm, on the same thread and sharing the same stance (p. 17, Section 4.2.3). Pair enumeration, aggregation, and number of pairs are not stated.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (p. 18, Table 8). No participant-clustered uncertainty, bootstrap, SE, or CI is reported; exact dependence handling is not described.
diversity_detail.notes: Raw similarity would require sign reversal for the atlas diversity direction. No effect is computed here. The vocabulary has no means-only category: statistics_available none indicates absent precision/test statistics, not absent arm averages.

outcomes.name: Human-rated constructiveness: AI-assisted versus independent comments
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Separate Prolific raters selected the more constructive of two comments written for the same thread from the same stance. There were 401 HAI-versus-Human pair evaluations in the linked S5 rating dataset (pp. 12, 14-15); pair means a judged pair and does not establish the number of unique pairs. Constructiveness is output quality, not an explicit creativity score. The printed chi-square N=802 is not a people count. Bonferroni corrections were applied, but no participant-, comment-, or rater-clustered precision is stated. The Indian N=205 is retained as printed, with its denominator unresolved.

contrasts.reported: HAI preferred in 64% versus Human in 36%; χ²(1, N=802)=62.56, p<0.000005, φ=0.28, odds ratio=3.19. India: HAI 66% versus Human 34%, χ²(1, N=205)=39.96, p<0.000005, φ=0.31. US: HAI 62% versus Human 38%, χ²(1, N=392)=22.54, p<0.000005, φ=0.24. Indian N is transcribed as printed and requires clarification.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Section 4.2.1 for 401 pair evaluations; p. 15, Table 6, Figure 4, and Section 4.2.1.

outcomes.name: Lexical overlap across writers: cosine similarity and ROUGE-L
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Two reported lexical-overlap variants are retained together: cosine similarity of word-count vectors and ROUGE-L longest common subsequence overlap (pp. 17-19, Table 8). Methods name CountVectorizer for cosine similarity in the draft-final analysis (p. 12); Section 4.2.3 does not independently restate that implementation. Cosine is not treated as an embedding measure. Separate component results are preserved in reported: cosine shows no significant difference, whereas lower ROUGE-L with AI corresponds to greater cross-writer diversity. The statistical observation unit is not specified: the source does not establish whether the Mann-Whitney tests use individual text-pair scores or aggregated similarities, so unit and n_units are null.

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: control 0.33, test 0.30; statistics column is a dash and text reports no significant difference. Rogue-L: control 0.18, test 0.16; U=42029, Z=-3.73, p<0.001, r=0.16. Raw overlap is lower with AI for both variants, but a significant difference is reported only for ROUGE-L. Lower overlap corresponds to higher diversity.
contrasts.locator: pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of word-count vectors; ROUGE-L longest common subsequence.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: No embedding model: CountVectorizer is named for cosine in Methods (p. 12), without a separate implementation statement for Section 4.2.3; ROUGE-L is lexical overlap.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Different writers within the same arm, on the same thread and sharing the same stance (p. 17, Section 4.2.3). Pair enumeration, aggregation, and number of pairs are not stated.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (p. 18, Table 8). No participant-clustered uncertainty, bootstrap, SE, or CI is reported; exact dependence handling is not described.
diversity_detail.notes: Diversity direction reverses the raw overlap sign. Mixed denotes different statistical findings across variants, not opposite point-estimate directions.

outcomes.name: Vocabulary diversity: distinct-2 and type-token ratio (aggregation unclear)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Distinct-2 and TTR are retained together as vocabulary-diversity variants reported in Table 8 (p. 18). The paper does not state their formulas, independent observation unit, or whether it computes each metric within a comment or across a pooled corpus (pp. 17-19). Their status as diversity across different people cannot be confirmed. Conservatively retained as an ancillary output property (other, with_ai), with unit and n_units null; this provisional classification does not settle the aggregation question and is not used to establish diversity eligibility. Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections are reported, without participant-clustered precision.

contrasts.locator: p. 18, Table 8; p. 19, first paragraph of Section 4.2.3.

outcomes.name: Comment length
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Word count (p. 9, Table 3).  Tests use comment-level features. The paired comparison includes the subset incorporating AI; its people count is ambiguous (p. 16). Table 19 country-specific values are not pooled here. No participant-level SE is supplied. Length-adjusted tests are robustness analyses; any three-type omnibus effect is not an isolated randomized HAI-versus-Human effect. The randomized contrast uses final comments; the initial-to-final contrast is a fixed-order comparison within the AI arm, restricted to incorporated suggestions. The paper calls this subset 87 participants (p. 16), but its independent people count is not established. AI remains available during final writing, so these are not after_ai outcomes. The methods report 104 control and 102 test comments overall (p. 12), without giving an analysis-specific denominator for every feature. Measure code is null because the codebook defines automated_score as a creativity-scoring model and supplies no code for this computed text property; the source-supported method above is retained.

contrasts.reported: Table 15 prints a dash for HAI vs. Human on Length; Figure 5 shows no significant HAI-versus-Human difference for this feature. No exact nonsignificant p-value is supplied. Table 19 values: Control India 75, US 68; test India 74, US 70 (words).
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Figure 5 and Section 4.2.1; p. 32, Table 15; p. 33, Table 19.

eligibility.reason: S4 is an original online randomized experiment: individual writers were randomly assigned to independent writing without external assistance or GPT-4 revision assistance (p. 10, Section 3.2). The analyzed writing sample is 103 people, supported by the Introduction and Table 5 (52 US and 51 Indian participants; pp. 2, 12), exceeding 50 despite the unexplained difference from recruitment. Section 4.2.3 explicitly compares final comments by different participants on the same thread and with the same stance; Table 8 reports semantic similarity, cosine similarity, and ROUGE-L computed on those outputs (pp. 17-19). GPT-4 remained available until final submission (p. 11, Figure 2). These cross-writer outcomes meet criterion 3 even though their statistical observation units and dependence handling are unspecified. Distinct-2/TTR, ancillary text properties, preparatory annotation studies, and evaluation-panel sizes are unnecessary to establish the three criteria. S5 supplies linked AI-only-versus-human context evidence and is not a second eligible writing experiment. None of the remaining source questions changes the eligibility decision.

one_line_finding: Among 103 analyzed writers (pp. 2, 12), AI-assisted comments showed no significant semantic-similarity difference (0.42 vs. 0.41) but lower ROUGE-L overlap (0.16 vs. 0.18; U=42029, p<0.001, r=0.16; p. 18, Table 8), and were preferred as more constructive in 64% of paired judgments (p. 15, Figure 4).
open_questions: Distinct-2 and TTR: the independent analysis unit and within-comment versus across-comment aggregation are unspecified; across-person diversity cannot be confirmed (pp. 17-19, Table 8).

Writer recruitment reports 52 Indian and 52 US people, whereas the analyzed writing sample is 103: Table 5 lists 51 Indian and 52 US participants who completed the task, consistent with the Introduction. The reason for the difference, assignment-stage count, and people counts by arm are not stated (pp. 2, 12).

The incorporation analysis refers to 87 participants within the test arm. Its independent people denominator and whether 87 refers to people, comments, or writing tasks cannot be reconciled with the reported writer and output counts; do not use 87 as a verified people count (pp. 10, 12, 16).

Cross-writer similarity: the statistical observation unit, pair counts, exact enumeration/aggregation, and treatment of dependence among pairs or repeated comments/writers are not stated. No participant-level SE, SD, or CI is supplied (pp. 17-19).

The evaluation methods specify four pairs per rater but report 727 evaluations from 157 analyzed raters. Table 6 prints N=802 for 401 HAI-versus-Human evaluations and N=205 for its Indian subgroup; the chi-square construction and inconsistent denominators are not explained (pp. 12, 14-15).

The validation prose reports a final stimulus pool of 32 comments per country, while Table 2 reports 39 US comments meeting the validation criterion. Selection of the final subset is not described (pp. 8-9).
For HAI-versus-AI constructiveness, the prose reports AI preference in 55% of cases, whereas Figure 4 prints 56%; this non-core contrast is not silently corrected (p. 15).
No study-specific data/code release URL or preregistration is identified in the saved document. Generic software/model links on p. 12 are not study data/code releases.
S1 validation randomly samples four comments per annotator, but exposure to both argumentation styles and their order are not established (pp. 7-8; no clarification in Appendix A).

Within-writer draft-final content retention: the number of analyzed pairs and inferential precision are not established; the ambiguous incorporation-subset count does not supply a verified pair or people denominator (pp. 12, 16-18, Figure 6A). These ancillary results remain in notes under the outcome cap.

Manual opinion-distortion coding reports 12 instances (12.7%), but the denominator, coding protocol, and whether those rewrites were accepted as final submissions are not stated (p. 19, Section 4.2.4). This ancillary result remains in notes under the outcome cap.
The saved document is arXiv:2411.03295v5 with ACM journal formatting; equivalence to the publisher version of record has not been independently established (p. 1).

The measure vocabulary has no matching code for the non-creativity text properties in S4-O5 through S4-O14. Their methods are documented, but any future code assignment requires a vocabulary decision rather than additional source evidence.
notes: Finalized 2026-10-09. Checked all three challenge files against the full document and the current form specification/codebook. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the prior review record; final decisions govern the current study fields. Read all 1074 markdown lines, including references and Appendix A; checked retained numbers and eligibility evidence against physical PDF pages and extracted Tables 2-6, 8, and 15-19 with PyMuPDF. Locators are 1-based PDF pages. The saved file is arXiv v5 with ACM journal formatting, not independently verified as the publisher version of record. Five entries preserve preparatory validation (S1), the questionnaire pilot (S2), perception experiment (S3), randomized writers (S4), and a linked evaluation/AI-only benchmark (S5). Only S4 determines core eligibility; the final-summary people count is 103 analyzed writers, not the larger annotator panel or the sum of panels. S2 total 49 is the exact sum of printed US 27 and India 22; S3 analyzed total 99 is supported by the printed US 50 and India 49 and by 103 participants minus four exclusions (p. 10). No writer arm counts are derived from comment counts, and the abstract aggregate of 600 is not used for eligibility. The final form preserves 15 outcome entries: 14 assisted-writing outcomes and one linked AI-only benchmark. Cosine/ROUGE-L are grouped as lexical-overlap variants with separate component results; distinct-2/TTR are grouped as vocabulary-diversity variants with unresolved aggregation. Named entities and the AI-only benchmark, recorded only by B, are retained. Under form-spec.md Rule 7, the main 15 outcome entries are retained and two additional ancillary analyses are described here rather than added as separate entries. Within-writer draft-final content retention has reported mean semantic similarity 0.67, BERTScore 0.87, and cosine similarity 0.38 (p. 17, Section 4.2.2; methods p. 12; Figure 6A p. 18). These scores compare each initial draft with its final AI-assisted submission; they are other/with_ai fidelity evidence, not across-person diversity or a randomized between-arm effect. The analyzed pair count and inferential precision are not established. Manual review identified 12 instances (12.7%) in which the LLM changed the original opinion (p. 19, Section 4.2.4, Editing). This is output-based fidelity evidence, not just participant self-report; its denominator, coding protocol, and acceptance into final submissions are not established. No denominator is derived from the count and percentage. The challenges correctly identify both analyses in the paper, but their omission as separate outcome entries complies with the explicit outcome cap. AI-only linguistic comparisons and logical/dialectical stimulus checks are not duplicated as assistance outcomes. Self-reported satisfaction, ownership, difficulty, prompt choices, and writing time are not scored creative outputs. Within-test draft-final and editing comparisons are before_after within the AI-available session, not randomized contrasts or after_ai evidence. No explicit primary-outcome or preregistration designation was found. For statistics_available, figure_only denotes graphical distributions/significance information when tables print a dash and no numeric contrast test; printed country-specific descriptive values are also retained. The none code for semantic similarity denotes lack of numeric test/precision statistics, not absence of arm averages. Omnibus three-comment-type ANCOVAs are retained as robustness information, not isolated randomized assistance effects. No effect sizes or uncertainty estimates were computed. n_unresolved counts unresolved substantive screener differences; shared source limitations remain in open_questions. S1 assignment.structure and S4-O1/S4-O3 analysis units are null because the corresponding methods are not explicit. S4-O5 through S4-O14 retain their verified text-property methods and results with measure null; automated_score is restricted to creativity-scoring models by codebook Section 6. Challenge counts refer to the six submitted problems, not individual fields changed; n_open counts unresolved challenges, while final.open_items separately records remaining source limitations. Counts after exclusions are described as analyzed. No reanalysis of another paper is identified, so S4 remains online_rct.

open_items.item: Distinct-2/TTR aggregation and observation unit remain unresolved (open_questions[0] and the unresolved reconciliation difference for S4-O4). Analysis code defining per-comment versus pooled computation would settle this. Criterion 3 is already met by S4-O1/S4-O3, so the provisional other/with_ai coding does not affect eligibility.

The recruitment-versus-analysis discrepancy and assignment-stage/per-arm people counts need participant-flow and allocation clarification from the authors (pp. 2, 12). Criterion 2 is met by the independently documented 103 analyzed writers.

The incorporation-subset label of 87 participants needs author clarification of whether it counts people, comments, or tasks (p. 16). It concerns ancillary within-arm analyses and does not replace the 103-person analyzed writing sample for criterion 2.

Cross-writer similarity needs analysis code and participant-linked output data to establish statistical units, pair enumeration, aggregation, dependence handling, and participant-level precision (pp. 17-19). This affects quantitative synthesis, while criterion 3 is already met by computed comparisons across different writers.

The four-pairs-per-rater procedure, 727 evaluations from 157 analyzed raters, and Table 6 chi-square denominators need the authors to clarify the evaluation allocation and contingency tables (pp. 12, 14-15). These are evaluation counts, not the criterion-2 writer sample; diversity independently establishes criterion 3.

The 32 final US validation comments versus 39 comments meeting the validation criterion require the authors to identify the selected stimulus subset (pp. 8-9). This preparatory stimulus-selection issue affects no eligibility criterion.

The HAI-versus-AI preference of 55% in prose versus 56% in Figure 4 needs author clarification of the correct numerator and denominator (p. 15). This is a non-core contrast and affects no eligibility criterion.

No study-specific data/code release URL or preregistration is identified in the saved document. The authors could supply any release or registration and its status; neither is required by the three eligibility criteria.

S1 exposure to both argumentation styles and their order would require the validation protocol or author clarification (pp. 7-8). Structure is conservatively null, and S1 does not determine any core criterion.

The analyzed draft-final pair count and uncertainty for content-retention scores would require participant-linked pairs and analysis code (pp. 12, 16-18). These ancillary fidelity summaries are not used for any eligibility criterion.

The denominator, coding protocol, and final-submission status behind 12 opinion-distortion instances (12.7%) require author clarification (p. 19). This ancillary fidelity result is not used for any eligibility criterion.
Equivalence between the saved arXiv v5 and the publisher version of record requires comparison with the journal version. No version-dependent eligibility conflict is identified in the saved document.

S4-O5 through S4-O14 have verified methods but no matching measure code in the current vocabulary. Null codes and explicit method descriptions complete screening; a future vocabulary decision requires no further paper evidence and affects no eligibility criterion.
